papers.title: Persistent cerebrovascular injury after preeclampsia in the STOX1A mouse model: implications for prokineticin signaling
papers.abstract: Preeclampsia (PE) is a pregnancy-related hypertensive disorder associated with neurological complications that may persist beyond pregnancy. Prokineticins (PROK1 and PROK2) and their receptors (PROKR1 and PROKR2) regulate angiogenesis and inflammation and may be involved to PE-associated cerebrovascular injury. This study investigated alterations of the maternal brain prokineticin system during PE and 8 months postpartum, and assessed the consequences of prokineticin receptor inhibition using the PROKR antagonist PC1. Female WT FVB/N mice mated with transgenic males overexpressing STOX1A were used as a model of PE and received PC1 or vehicle during gestation. Circulating and regional brain PROK levels and receptor expression were assessed by ELISA and Western blotting. Long-term cerebral abnormalities were evaluated using high-resolution MRI and GFAP immunostaining. PE mice exhibited hypertension, proteinuria, reduced placental efficiency, and elevated circulating PROK1 and PROK2 levels. PC1 prevented hypertension and attenuated the elevation of circulating PROKs but did not prevent proteinuria or reduced placental efficiency. During PE, hippocampal PROK1 increased while PROK2 decreased; these changes persisted despite treatment. At 7 months postpartum, both PROKs were elevated in the cortex, and these increases were prevented by PC1. Region-specific changes in PROKR1 immunoreactivity and PROKR2 expression showed variable responses to treatment. MRI revealed hippocampal and parieto-temporal T2* hypointensities compatible with microhemorrhagic injury, post-contrast T1 abnormalities supporting blood-brain barrier disruption, and a distinct caudoputamen T1-hyperintense lesion potentially representing a nonhemorrhagic component. PC1 prevented focal cerebral lesions and associated astrocyte reactivity, whereas regional diffusion abnormalities persisted. These findings implicate prokineticin signaling in persistent PE-associated brain injury and support the potential of receptor antagonism to limit selected cerebral alterations.

papers.title: Pre-stress functional brain connectivity is associated with subsequent anxiety during war-related stress
papers.abstract: Individuals exposed to major real-world stressors show markedly different psychological outcomes, but whether this heterogeneity is associated with pre-existing neural characteristics remains unclear because neuroimaging is rarely performed beforehand. We acquired resting-state fMRI in healthy adults before the unforeseen onset of war-related stress. Approximately 13 months later, during ongoing war-related stress, participants (n = 31) were assessed for anxiety, depressive symptoms, perceived stress and post-traumatic stress symptoms. Among 144 associations spanning 36 predefined corticolimbic and reward-related connections and four outcomes, lower baseline functional connectivity between the right nucleus accumbens and right amygdala was associated with greater subsequent anxiety. This association survived permutation-based family-wise error correction and adjustment for baseline depressive symptoms, age and sex. These findings provide preliminary prospective evidence that pre-existing functional organization of threat- and reward-related circuitry is associated with individual differences in anxiety during prolonged adversity.

papers.title: Neuroinflammation is an early pathological process in a mouse model of prodromal Parkinsons disease
papers.abstract: Approximately 90% of Parkinson's disease (PD) patients exhibit olfactory deficits, which often precedes motor symptoms by years, and are a robust predictor for PD and subsequent cognitive decline. Pathological changes in the PD olfactory system, particularly synuclein (Syn) pathology in the olfactory bulb (OB) and severe involvement of the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON), are distinct from normal aging. However, the causal link between Syn aggregation and functional impairment, potentially involving cytotoxicity and neuroinflammation, remains elusive. To investigate these early pathological events, we utilized a prodromal PD model that we have previously characterized, involving the unilateral OB injection of Syn preformed fibrils (PFF) in wild-type mice. This triggers the transneuronal spread of pathogenic Syn, and olfactory dysfunction starting at 1-month post-injections. Here we report on neuropathological and inflammatory events 1-3 month following injection of PFFs into the OB. Following PFF injection, Syn pSer129 pathology progressively accumulated bilaterally in the AON and ipsilateral in the piriform cortex (PCX) over three months. Stereological quantification revealed no significant neuronal loss in the AON or PCX during this 1-3 month interval, indicating that olfactory impairment precedes overt neurodegeneration. Instead, we identified the upregulation of pro-inflammatory genes (Il-1{beta} ; and Il-6), significant microglial reactivity, and sustained astrogliosis within olfactory structures. These findings identify neuroinflammation as a key early mediator linking Syn pathology to olfactory dysfunction in the absence of neuronal loss. This suggests a critical window for therapeutic intervention and highlights neuroinflammatory markers as potential biomarkers for the prodromal phase of PD.

papers.title: Goat Milk-derived Extracellular Vesicles modulate glial responses in vitro and attenuate neuroinflammation in vivo
papers.abstract: Milk-derived extracellular vesicles (MEV) represent a naturally derived, potentially scalable platform for immunomodulation, yet their effects on central nervous system (CNS) glial inflammation at defined particle-to-cell ratios remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we investigated the immunomodulatory effects of goat milk-derived MEV in cellular and murine models of neuroinflammation. MEV-enriched preparations were obtained by sequential filtration, ultrafiltration, and size-exclusion chromatography, and characterized by scanning electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and dynamic light scattering. In LPS-stimulated BV2 microglia-like cells, MEV at 250 and 2500 particles per cell significantly reduced CD40 expression. In primary rat mixed glial cultures, microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes internalized MEV. At 250 particles per cell, MEV significantly reduced CD40 and IL1{beta} gene expression at the mixed-culture level. In both cellular models, MEV also increased markers associated with an M2-like microglial phenotype under resting conditions. Following intrathecal administration in healthy mice, MEV did not induce significant changes in the inflammatory gene markers assessed at 8 h. In an LPS-induced mouse model of neuroinflammation, intrathecal MEV administration reduced CD40 protein expression towards control levels within 24 h and shifted the inflammatory marker profile towards a pro-resolutive state, as indicated by increased Arg1 levels and elevated CD206/CD86 and IL10/IL6 ratios. These findings identify goat milk-derived MEV-enriched preparations as potential modulators of CNS glial inflammation and support further investigation of their therapeutic potential.

papers.title: Spatially resolved single-cell atlas reveals cortical glial reactivity associated with regions of neuronal growth programs in both hemispheres after stroke
papers.abstract: Post-stroke recovery relies on structural remodeling of neuronal circuits in both the spared ipsilesional and contralesional cortices. RNA sequencing studies have identified distinct states of glial reactivity after stroke, but how these states are spatially organized at the single-cell level in relation to neuronal responses remains unknown. Consequently, it remains unclear which reactive states are lesion-restricted versus remote regions, such as the contralesional cortex, and how remote glial responses relate to the neuronal growth programs that support circuit repair. To address this, we used imaging-based subcellular spatial transcriptomics to profile ~650,000 cells across both hemispheres in male and female mice 7 days after cortical ischemic stroke, a critical timepoint for neuroplasticity. Reactive glial states differed significantly in their spatial organization from the lesion: scar-forming astrocytes and infiltrating pro-inflammatory myeloid cells were confined to the perilesional rim, whereas a reactive microglial state and a reactive astrocyte state extended into remote gray and white matter of the contralesional hemisphere. Mapping neuronal growth-associated gene expression across the entire cortex, we found substantial activation in both the perilesional and homotopic contralesional cortex, and these same regions showed significantly increased proportions of reactive microglia and astrocytes. Together, these findings identify spatially organized neuronal growth and glial activation states in both hemispheres after stroke and nominate regions for investigating spatial relationships between complex cell types and functional recovery.

papers.title: Blue light compromises cellular fate of intrinsically photosensitive M&uumlller glial cells in the developing chicken retina.
papers.abstract: M&uumlller glial cells (MCs), the predominant glial population in the retina, interface with all neuronal types to form the structural and functional core of the tissue. Beyond their established homeostatic roles, MCs have emerged as promising endogenous neural stem cells with remarkable regenerative potential. Our recent work identified MCs as novel photosensitive elements of the vertebrate inner retina that express non-visual opsins and respond to brief light stimuli. Direct photic responses manifest as a sustained increase in intracellular calcium levels driven by a G protein-mediated signaling cascade that primarily recruits calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, highlighting MC photoreception and its roles in retinal physiology. In the present work, we characterize expanded light-directed responses in primary chicken MC cultures, identifying a blue light (BL)-triggered signaling cascade. BL stimulation induces a peak in cAMP levels at 10 min, followed by CREB activation (p-CREB) within 30 min, a temporal profile consistent with observations in ex vivo retinal explants. BL exposure (1 h) at the onset of each cell cycle dampens proliferative capacity and migration while lengthening the cell cycle in both primary chicken MCs and an immortalized human MC cell line compared to dark controls. Furthermore, over time (24, 48, and 72 h), BL exposure reduces the proportion of pluripotent cells (Sox2 positive cells), concomitant with an increase in neuronal progenitors (Tbr2) and no change in glial markers (GS, RGR, GFAP). Finally, mature neuronal markers (TUJ-1 and Brn3) increase in MC cultures 120 h post-BL stimulation. Overall, this work broadens our understanding of BL-triggered signaling cascades in MCs and uncovers photoreception as a potential mechanism driving cell fate in the developing retina.

papers.title: Impact of heat and sex on embryonic brain growth in dragons with temperature induced sex-reversal (Pogona vitticeps, Lacertilia: Agamidae)
papers.abstract: Climate warming can influence sex determination and embryonic growth in oviparous reptiles that rely on external temperatures during development. Warmer incubation temperatures can stimulate growth in ectotherms until oxygen supply can no longer keep pace with growth rate; at which point metabolically expensive organs like the brain suffer. We aimed to understand the impact of heat and sex on brain development in central bearded dragons, Pogona vitticeps (Agamidae), a uniquely thermosensitive species that exhibits sex-reversal at warm incubation temperatures. Three sexual phenotypes are possible in P. vitticeps: genetically driven ZW females and ZZ males, with the latter phenotype thermally overridden at incubation temperatures >32C to induce ZZ sex-reversed females. To visualise changes in brain anatomy, we used buffered Lugols iodine to perform contrast-enhanced micro computed tomography (microCT) and synchrotron propagation-based phase-contrast CT scanning. A total of 57 embryos were sampled across developmental stages and incubated at two temperature treatments: cool (28C, n = 26) and warm (36C, n = 21). Using high-resolution models of neuroanatomy, we found that the telencephalic region of the forebrain is significantly larger in individuals with ZZ genotypes (males and sex-reversed females) compared to concordant ZW females. Although incubation temperature significantly influenced growth rate and body size during development, overall brain size was not significantly different across temperature treatments. Our results indicate that the effects of genotypic sex on brain development are more important than thermal influences, and thus the brain may be somewhat buffered to the effects of warm incubation temperatures in this arid-adapted dragon.

papers.title: Imbalance between RNA-binding proteins and the WAVE regulatory complex underlies the toxic gain-of-function effects of the CYFIP2 Arg87Cys variant in neurodevelopmental disorders
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants in cytoplasmic FMR1-interacting protein 2 (CYFIP2) cause neurodevelopmental disorders, with hotspot substitutions at arginine 87 (Arg87) associated with particularly severe symptoms. CYFIP2 functions both as a component of the WAVE (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein family verprolin-homologous protein) regulatory complex (WRC), regulating the actin cytoskeleton, and as an interactor of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) involved in mRNA processing/translation. Although Arg87 variants reduce CYFIP2 protein stability, heterozygous knock-in mice carrying Arg87Cys (Cyfip2+/R87C) show markedly more severe phenotypes than heterozygous knockout (Cyfip2+/-) mice, supporting a toxic gain-of-function mechanism. However, how the dual roles of CYFIP2 contribute to this mechanism remains unclear. To address this, we examined Cyfip2+/R87C mice at postnatal week 7, before overt neuronal loss and gliosis, focusing on the progressive dispersion of hippocampal cornu ammonis 1 (CA1) pyramidal neurons, a phenotype absent in Cyfip2+/- mice. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing suggested candidate alterations related to translation and cell adhesion/migration in CA1 pyramidal neurons. Complementarily, human embryonic kidney 293T cells expressing CYFIP2 Arg87Cys showed defects in proliferation and morphology, accompanied by altered expression of cell adhesion-related genes. Quantitative proteomic analysis of the CA1 region uncovered an imbalance between CYFIP2-associated protein networks, characterized by increased RBPs and reduced WRC components. Phosphoproteomic analysis further revealed altered phosphorylation of synaptic and translational regulators. Consistently, whole-cell recordings and biocytin-based morphological analyses showed increased frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents and altered dendritic morphology in Cyfip2+/R87C CA1 pyramidal neurons, most prominently in the more severely dispersed deep-layer neurons. Moreover, the cell adhesion molecule Eph receptor A3 was reduced, possibly as a result of RBP dysregulation. Together, these findings suggest that an imbalance between RBP- and WRC-associated pathways underlies the gain-of-function effects of CYFIP2 Arg87Cys and contributes to early neuronal phenotypes, most notably CA1 layer dispersion. This mechanism, distinct from CYFIP2 haploinsufficiency, supports allele-specific therapeutic strategies for Arg87 variants.

papers.title: Coordinated orienting behavior emerges following unilateral optogenetic activation of Superior Colliculus GABAergic neurons
papers.abstract: Orienting coordinates movements of the eyes, whiskers, nose, and other effectors, but how the superior colliculus (SC) recruits these components over time remains unclear. We combined unilateral optogenetic activation of SC GABAergic neurons with high-speed tracking of facial movements and Neuropixels recordings to examine SC-evoked orienting in head-fixed mice. Stimulation recruited movements of the whiskers, nose, eyes, and pupil. Horizontal eye and nose movements were directed contralateral to the stimulated hemisphere, whereas vertical eye movements, pupil dilation, and whisker protraction did not differ significantly between stimulation sides. Nose and whisker movements generally preceded eye movements, followed by slower pupil dilation, revealing a temporally organized response. Recordings from the SC contralateral to the stimulated hemisphere revealed heterogeneous neuronal responses comprising short-latency excitation and delayed excitation or inhibition. Short-latency excitation was similar on trials with and without evoked movements, whereas delayed excitation was greater on trials that evoked eye or nose movements. Neurons modulated during spontaneous nose movements showed corresponding optogenetically evoked responses, linking stimulation-induced activity to endogenous movement-related activity. Thus, activation of SC GABAergic neurons initiates evolving population activity that recruits a coordinated sequence of orienting movements.

papers.title: Accumulation of FAM98B and tRNA-Splicing Ligase Complex Proteins in Neuronal Intranuclear Inclusions in Spinocerebellar ataxia type 4.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 4 (SCA4) is caused by a GGC-repeat expansion in ZFHX3 encoding an expanded polyglycine tract causing p62- and ubiquitin-positive neuronal intranuclear inclusions (NIIs). In multiple polyglycine diseases NIIs sequester tRNA-splicing ligase complex (tRNA-LC) proteins, causing downstream functional defects linked to neurodegeneration. We assessed the localization of tRNA-LC proteins in SCA4 pontine neurons. Methods: Postmortem brain tissue from a genetically confirmed SCA4 patient was examined across multiple regions using immunofluorescence confocal microscopy for p62, ubiquitin and tRNA-LC proteins FAM98B, RTRAF, and RTCB. Results: In pontine neurons, FAM98B, RTRAF, and RTCB were incorporated into NII, accumulating in a distinct outer layer respective to a ubiquitin inner layer. This redistribution was accompanied by depletion of all three proteins from the soluble nucleoplasm. Discussion: Our findings link SCA4 to a tRNA-LC dysfunction phenotype shared by multiple GGC-repeat disorders, further supporting a unified pathological mechanism in polyglycine diseases.

papers.title: Projection Neurons from Infralimbic (IL) to the Basolateral Amygdala (BLA) are Critical for the Expression of Social Familiarity induced Anxiolysis (SoFiA) in rats
papers.abstract: Mental health is crucially linked to social behavior. Healthy social behavior involves learning to adapt emotional responses to social cues, for example learning to suppress anxiety through social familiarity, or social familiarity-induced anxiolysis (SoFiA). SoFiA is well documented and forms the basis for interpersonal therapy, however, the neural mechanisms of SoFiA are unclear. SoFiA is modeled in rats by employing the social interaction habituation (SI-hab) protocol. Using SI-hab protocol, it has been determined that SoFiA represents social safety learning, which requires both anxiogenic stimulus and social familiarity during training sessions (5-6 daily SI sessions), and SoFiA expression is dependent on infralimbic subdivision (IL) of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the basolateral amygdala (BLA). Here we investigated the role of IL in SoFiA acquisition and expression, using chemogenetics to inhibit IL neurons. Male Wistar rats received bilateral viral injections targeting the IL or BLA and left undisturbed for 5-7 weeks to allow for viral expression. We chemogenetically inhibited via low doses of ip. clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) either the IL, the BLA, or the projections neurons from the IL to the BLA during expression of SoFiA in rats. We found that projection neurons from IL to the BLA are critical for the recovery SI behavior from the attenuation caused by the bright light (expression of SoFiA). Furthermore, CNO inhibited IL neurons with projections to the BLA and there were no off target effects of CNO on the behavioral measures. These results suggest an essential role of the IL-BLA pathway in social safety learning.

papers.title: Movement refinement and cholinergic regulation of outcome-dependent updating during skilled reaching.
papers.abstract: Motor skill learning transforms initially variable actions into precise and reproducible movements, yet conventional measures of task success can obscure the distinct processes through which this refinement occurs. We combined detailed outcome scoring and kinematic analysis of single-pellet reaching in mice to resolve how individual components of the action change with practice. Decomposing reaching into successive stages revealed improvements in targeting and retrieval, while grasp success after pellet contact did not change detectably. Paw trajectories became more consistent across both successful and unsuccessful reaches, whereas changes in the mean speed profile were detected in successful reaches. To examine how striatal cholinergic signaling contributes to movement refinement and the influence of recent outcomes on subsequent actions, we monitored acetylcholine (ACh) in vivo and inhibited cholinergic interneurons (CINs) during training. ACh was elevated before reach onset and declined during execution across all reach outcomes, with no detectable change between early and late training. CIN inhibition had little effect on movement refinement across days, but altered how recent outcomes influenced the next reach, most clearly following attempts in which the pellet was grasped and then lost. These findings distinguish refinement of the practiced movement from outcome-dependent adjustments to its execution. Together, they raise the possibility that the pre-reach ACh elevation plays a role in enabling the evaluation of recent outcomes to update the execution of the next reach.

papers.title: The human circular Tau 12->7 RNA is translated in mouse neurons and promotes tau aggregation
papers.abstract: In addition to numerous mRNA isoforms, the human microtubule associated protein tau (MAPT) gene generates circular RNAs that are not known to be expressed in rodents. Using adeno associated viruses, we expressed human circular Tau RNA generated from backsplicing of exon 12 to exon 7 (circTau 12->7) in mouse brain. We observed rolling circle translation of circTau 12->7, similar to cultured human HEK293 cells. Despite using a ubiquitously active promoter, circTau 12->7 protein and a control circEGFP protein were only observed in mouse neurons, indicating neuron-specific translation of these circular RNAs. CircTau 12->7 expression resulted in tau aggregates resembling neurofibrillary tangles in mouse brain that included endogenous mouse tau protein. Our data support a model where neuron-specific translation of circTau RNAs induces 'linear', mRNA-translated tau aggregation, which could contribute to tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease. Thus, targeting circTau RNAs could be a therapeutic approach for Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: Direct cortical feedforward and feedback pathways differentially shape visual responses and selectively engage looped circuits
papers.abstract: Nearly every computational account of hierarchical cortex rests on assumptions about the influence of direct cortico-cortical inputs and which neurons they act upon. Yet, disentangling their direct functional contributions from indirect, multisynaptic influences remains difficult. We examined how feedforward (FF) and feedback (FB) pathways between mouse primary visual cortex (V1) and posteromedial cortex (PM) modulate visual responses, combining retrograde labelling, multi-area two-photon imaging and optogenetic perturbations. High or low activity in either pathway was associated with both excitation and inhibition of neurons in the targeted areas. FF activity was associated with stronger additive changes, while FB activity was related to stronger multiplicative modulations and improvements in visual decoding. Optogenetic manipulations causally confirmed these asymmetries. Both pathways preferentially modulated reciprocating "looped" neurons, with FF exciting them and FB either exciting or inhibiting them. These findings demonstrate that feedforward and feedback pathways serve distinct functional roles within recurrent cortical loops.

papers.title: Odor representations are structured by heterogeneous tuning and concentration-dependence of functionally distinct olfactory sensory neuron subpopulations.
papers.abstract: Olfactory stimuli (odorants) are represented by combinatorial patterns of olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) activation that are translated into spatially-organized glomerular maps at their input to the CNS. How glomerular maps relate to odorant features - including chemical structure and concentration - remains a key question in understanding the neural mechanisms of odor coding. Here, we compared glomerular response maps for the same 59 odorants across three concentration regimes, using GCaMP6 imaging from OSN axon terminals in the olfactory bulb (OB) of the anesthetized mouse. At the lowest regime, in which concentrations were chosen to distinguish the most sensitive glomeruli for each odorant, glomeruli were exceptionally narrowly tuned and responses across glomeruli were extremely sparse. We then compared responses at two higher-concentration regimes, 'low' and 'high', differing by 25-fold from each other and 2 - 5 log units higher than the 'most-sensitive' regime. Increasing concentration broadened tuning of OSN inputs; this broadening was heterogeneous across chemical space and was well-described by classifying glomeruli into several subpopulations with distinct consensus tuning profiles. Each subpopulation was selectively tuned to one or a few odorant chemical classes and spatially clustered in a manner consistent with the projection patterns of receptor-defined OSN classes. Glomerular subpopulations retained distinct tuning and spatial localization even at the highest concentrations. OSN subpopulations thus sample chemical space nonuniformly across a large concentration range. These results suggest a lower-dimensional structure in the representation of odorant information that largely reflects OSN subpopulations which, in turn, map to olfactory receptor subfamilies. This organization may enable distinct odor coding strategies for different OSN classes and for parts of chemical feature space with distinct ethological relevance.

papers.title: The Parkinson's disease-associated A53E mutation decreases alpha-synuclein aggregation and phosphorylation in vivo
papers.abstract: Abnormal -synuclein aggregation is the defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD) and related synucleinopathies. Rare disease-causing alpha-synuclein mutations either accelerate or slow fibrillization in vitro, however their effects in vivo are less well understood. Interestingly, the A53E mutation slows fibrillization in vitro but causes a more virulent form of PD. We use an in vivo model to examine the aggregation dynamics of disease-causing A53E and E46K alpha-synuclein mutations. Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching within presynaptic terminals shows that A53E-alpha-synuclein is significantly more mobile than E46K- or wild-type (WT)-alpha-synuclein. Longitudinal analysis in vivo reveals that E46K- and WT-alpha-synuclein become progressively less mobile over days, while A53E maintains high mobility, suggesting delayed progression toward aggregated states. We also find that A53E-alpha-synuclein lacks detectable disease-relevant phosphorylation at serine-129, unlike E46K-and WT-alpha-synuclein. To mechanistically test whether this unique lack of phosphorylation drives its high mobility, we genetically modified A53E-alpha-synuclein to mimic S129 phosphorylation, and show that this manipulation indeed decreases its mobility, directly implicating the phosphorylation status of this residue in mobility.

papers.title: Alterations in phototransduction timing, dark adaptation and GNAT1 trafficking in GNAT1-edited Xenopus laevis.
papers.abstract: GNAT1 (also called -transducin) is the -subunit of a heterotrimeric G-protein present in rod photoreceptors that plays a critical role in phototransduction. Photoactivated rhodopsin binds GNAT1, which stimulates phosphodiesterase to hydrolyze cGMP, closing ion channels and hyperpolarizing the rod cell. To examine the effects of GNAT1 ablation on light-induced autophagy and light-exacerbated retinal degeneration, we previously generated genetically chimeric, GNAT1-edited Xenopus laevis using CRISPR technology. Here, we interbred these F0 animals to produce F1 animals with defined genotypes, including full knockouts, and characterized the F1 generation by Western blot, histology, and electroretinography (ERG). In X. laevis tadpoles with nonsense mutations in all four GNAT1 alleles, the GNAT1 protein was absent, and the scotopic ERG was absent, indicating full knockout. In animals with reduced GNAT1 expression, we observed increased A- and B-wave implicit times. Greater GNAT1 protein reduction was associated with greater ERG delay, demonstrating a role for GNAT1 in the timing of phototransduction. We also identified two unexpected phenotypes linked to distinct gene edits. The Q184L-GNAT1.L mutation conferred an ERG phenotype similar to that of a full knockout, but with minimal reduction in GNAT1 protein levels, consistent with loss of function. This mutation is also present in the human population. A three-base-pair deletion (T183,Q184[->]K183) in GNAT1.S caused dominantly inherited diminished ERG response and defective dark adaptation, and was associated with photoreceptor structural abnormalities and GNAT1 accumulation at the connecting cilium, consistent with a dominant-negative effect on GNAT1 trafficking.

papers.title: Defining cell type-specific diurnal gene expression in the mouse retina
papers.abstract: The mammalian retina exhibits daily oscillations in gene expression that contribute to retinal physiology and visual function. However, the extent to which these temporal patterns differ among retinal cell types remains incompletely understood. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing in the mouse retina over the day and night, identifying rhythmic genes in the six major retinal cell types. Distinct diurnal gene expression patterns across photoreceptors, interneurons, retinal ganglion cells, and Muller glia correspond to their diverse functions across the light cycle. Even core circadian clock genes exhibited differences in paralog expression and rhythmicity across the retina. In contrast, dopamine signaling via the DRD4 receptor is highly rhythmic across most retinal cell types, suggesting dopamine signaling may be a key rhythmicity cue in the retina under diurnal conditions. This dataset highlights the complexity of daily transcriptional regulation in the retina and provides a resource to explore cell-type-specific diurnal rhythms.

papers.title: Concussive Injury in Human Forebrain Organoids Alters Neurogenesis and Neuroimmune Signaling
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of long-term neurological disability, yet the mechanisms underlying human-specific injury responses remain poorly understood. Rodent models of TBI have yielded significant insights into mechanisms and pathophysiology of TBI but may not capture human-specific developmental and molecular responses. Here, we establish a human forebrain organoid (hFBO) injury paradigm to examine developmental stage and region-specific responses to concussive injury. Dorsal and ventral hFBOs, enriched in glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons, respectively, showed progressive physiological maturation with rudimentary firing characteristics at 80 days in vitro (DIV) and spontaneous synaptic activity by 150 DIV. Injury to dorsal and ventral hFBOs at 25 DIV, when neural progenitors dominate, caused cell death that scaled with severity and increased expression of neural proliferation markers and TLR4/NF-{kappa}B associated neuroimmune signaling. Injury to physiologically mature organoids at 150 DIV produced severity-dependent acute intracellular calcium dysregulation. Together, these findings establish a human organoid-based platform that captures developmental stage-dependent neurogenic, molecular, and cellular dysfunction in responses to concussive injury.

papers.title: TMEM106B C-Terminal fragment aggregation exacerbates α-synuclein and TDP-43 proteinopathy phenotypes.
papers.abstract: Genetic variation in the human gene encoding the lysosomal transmembrane protein 106B (TMEM106B) drives risk of neurodegenerative dementia. A C-terminal fragment of TMEM106B (TMEM CT) accumulates in lesions across neurodegenerative disease, potentially contributing to neurotoxicity and hampering efficacy of therapeutic interventions. Previously, we developed the first transgenic organism model of TMEM CT neuronal aggregation in Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans). We demonstrated that TMEM CT neuronal aggregation drives severe neuronal dysfunction and neuronal loss. To investigate the potential synergistic interaction of TMEM CT aggregation with other types of aggregated neurotoxic proteinopathies occurring in dementia, we assessed neuronal degeneration and pathogenic protein accumulation in bigenic C. elegans expressing TMEM CT and other key proteinopathies of neurodegeneration including a-synuclein, tau, and TAR DNA binding protein 43 (TDP-43). Our results showed strong neurotoxic synergy of TMEM106B with TDP-43 or -synuclein. However, we detected only mild synergy between TMEM106B and tau. This work provides evidence in support of TMEM CT aggregation as a significant participant in the neurodegenerative process attributed to other toxic protein aggregates. The work also highlights the importance of considering secondary proteinopathy contributions including TMEM CT aggregation when developing interventions against primary TDP-43 or -synuclein proteinopathies.

papers.title: Behavioral Markers of Essential Tremor Correlate with Distributed Alteration of Brain Functional Connectivity
papers.abstract: Essential Tremor (ET) is a common motor disorder characterized by involuntary oscillations of the upper limbs during voluntary movement. Although increasing evidence implicates dysfunction of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway, ET remains a diagnosis of exclusion, as no definitive biological marker currently exists. To better characterize ET, we recently hypothesized that impaired compensation of sensorimotor delays within the long-latency feedback pathways may generate the tremor-like oscillations observed in ET. This theory suggests that the mean spectral amplitude (MSA), derived from limb kinematics, may serve as a potential marker of ET. Here we investigated the relationship between MSA, standard clinical assessment (Fahn Tolosa Marin Tremor Rating Scale; FTM-TRS), and brain connectivity derived from resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). Using seed-based analyses, we replicated previous findings of reduced functional connectivity between the dentate nucleus and components of the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway in ET patients compared with neurologically intact (NI) age-matched participants. Graph-theoretical analyses of whole-brain functional networks revealed distributed alterations in network topology across motor-related cortical and subcortical regions. Several graph metrics correlated with FTM-TRS scores and/or MSA, particularly within motor-related cortical and subcortical circuits, including the thalamus, basal ganglia, and cerebellum in ET. These findings indicate that ET is characterized by distributed alterations in functional brain networks beyond reduced connectivity of dentate nucleus and highlights MSA as a candidate quantitative marker linking altered brain connectivity to sensorimotor delay-driven tremor oscillations.

papers.title: Brain and kidney Extracellular Vesicle Morphology and Complementary Brain proteomics after Inflammatory Challenge
papers.abstract: Shape, size variation, and protein composition describe different properties of tissue extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations. We compared brain and kidney EV shape and size using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). We also assessed repeated protein detection and reanalyzed a deposited brain proteomics cohort, with attribution to its original source. The study used intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and an intravenous miRNA-associated EV formulation. Each group contained three biological samples, as labelled in the source data. Source morphometry summaries included 385 brain and 101 kidney profiles. Kidney circularity was 0.9225, 0.8977, and 0.9288 in the control, LPS, and treatment groups, respectively. The corresponding values for diameter quartile dispersion, a measure of size variation, were 0.2603, 0.5334, and 0.6018. Thus, near-control outline shape coexisted with persistent size variation. None of the six primary morphology tests remained significant after Holm correction. Independent recalculation confirmed 1,527 eligible rat protein accessions across individual searches. The complete quantitative matrix contained 953 features. The main peptide filter combined unique and razor peptides. A stricter analysis retained 916 features. PTGFRN and LAMB2 remained the only significant treatment-versus-LPS findings. In the main analysis, PTGFRN increased 14.71-fold (q = 0.0365), and LAMB2 increased 6.23-fold (q = 0.00585). Their LPS levels were already close to control values. Exploratory normalization used the geometric mean of four measured EV-associated markers. The resulting treatment-versus-LPS increases were 16.43-fold and 6.96-fold, respectively. These ratios support selective changes in relative protein representation within the recovered mixture. They do not establish protein copies per EV. Analysis of the full protein profile and calibration of the complete selection process did not support an overall return to control. This study compares morphology and composition as separate outcomes. It identifies membrane and matrix associations as priorities for validation. Original TEM measurements were unavailable, sample matching remained unresolved, and kidney proteomics were absent. These limitations prevent causal conclusions and individual-sample comparisons between morphology and protein composition.

papers.title: Bridging Sensory Extraction and Decision Dynamics: Face Pareidolia Emergent from Bottom-Up and Top-Down Interactions
papers.abstract: Face pareidolia-the illusory perception of faces in everyday objects-provides a unique window into how the human brain resolves visual ambiguity. Whether pareidolia arises from bottom-up sensory processing or top-down, expectation-driven feedback, is currently debated. Here we recorded electroencephalography (EEG) while participants viewed rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) streams of images, each of which was an object-to-face morph generated along a 21-image continuum via text-to-image diffusion models. Time-resolved representational similarity analyses revealed a clear spatiotemporal dissociation, in which early occipitotemporal areas tracked physical feature changes linearly, while later frontocentral channels collapsed this structural gradient into a sharp, sigmoidal profile reflecting discrete categorical decisions (face-like versus object-like). To characterise information transmission between these regions, we implemented a novel transformation-based representational connectivity analysis. These analyses uncovered an initial feedforward flow of information that transferred and transformed posterior linear traces into anterior sigmoidal representations. Crucially, partitioning the image continuum revealed that unambiguous stimuli (faces or objects) were predominantly resolved via feedforward information flow, whereas ambiguous pareidolic images recruited prolonged top-down feedback. Furthermore, perceptual decision sensitivity was biased by animacy priors and directly predicted individual behavioural reaction times during the task. Together, the findings help reconcile prior debate by establishing that face pareidolia is neither a feedforward process nor an isolated top-down projection, but an active, multi-stage recurrent process driven by feedforward feature extraction and top-down categorical resolution.

papers.title: Representational geometry of punishment learning across basolateral amygdala neurons
papers.abstract: Punishment learning allows animals to suppress actions that cause harm while maintaining actions that earn reward. Although the basolateral amygdala is necessary for punishment learning, how its population activity changes across learning, and how this activity reflects an action's consequences, remain unknown. We used longitudinal calcium imaging to track 1,147 basolateral amygdala neurons in male mice across instrumental training, punishment, choice test, and punishment extinction. Punishment learning transformed basolateral amygdala neuron activity associated with the punished action. This activity diverged from that associated with the unpunished action and became aligned with activity evoked by the punisher itself. This alignment was action and contingency specific. It preserved the direction of individual neurons' responses to the punisher: neurons activated by the punisher become more activated by the punished action alone, whereas neurons inhibited by the punisher become more inhibited by the punished action alone. We then asked whether reward and punishment were encoded separately or on a common value dimension across basolateral amygdala neurons. Punishment added a strong shock component to action-related activity without reducing its reward component, while reward and shock themselves occupied largely orthogonal population directions. Thus, during punishment learning, basolateral amygdala population activity can encode opposing consequences of the same action instead of simply changing what that action is worth.

papers.title: Mental replay rescales the subjective duration of past events via alpha and theta oscillations
papers.abstract: Human memory recall is flexible in time, allowing past events to be mentally replayed at variable speeds. However, it remains unclear whether temporally rescaled replay distorts the perceived duration of remembered events, and whether such distortion is tied to changes in the retrieved content. Here we instructed participants to mentally replay previously encoded naturalistic videos at compressed, expanded, or self-paced (free) speeds while recording scalp electroencephalography (EEG). Replaying an event at an expanded pace lengthened participants' subsequent judgments of its original duration relative to free and compressed replay, and the longer an event had been replayed, the longer it was judged to have lasted. Crucially, recalled memory content was unaffected, with gist accuracy and recalled detail comparable across speed conditions. During replay, alpha and theta power were reduced under compression, and both interacted with the speed instruction in predicting reported duration. Specifically, alpha power exhibited a stronger positive relationship with duration judgments under compressed replay than under free or expanded replay. Conversely, the relationship between theta power and reported duration was significantly more positive under expanded replay than under free or compressed replay. Neural pattern similarity between instructed and later spontaneous replay varied with replay speed, yet this reinstatement neither predicted reported duration nor mediated the oscillatory effects. These findings suggest that remembered duration is not read out from the amount of content retrieved but reconstructed at retrieval through oscillatory dynamics, decoupling the subjective scaling of time from the content of memory.

papers.title: Rapid switching of in-phase and anti-phase interhemispheric rhythms within a single theta cycle: a mechanistic explanation
papers.abstract: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) supports memory consolidation and spatial navigation. In vivo recordings of local field potential (LFP) from RSG reveal coexisting gamma (30-80 Hz) and spline (100-160 Hz) oscillations, coupled to distinct phases of the background theta ([~]8 Hz) rhythm. Remarkably, bilateral recordings reveal that gamma and splines exhibit divergent interhemispheric phase relationships: gamma is in-phase across hemispheres, while splines are anti-phase. Here, using numerical bifurcation analysis of next-generation neural mass models, we show that RSG oscillations within a single hemisphere can be understood as alternation of PING (pyramidal-interneuron gamma) and ING (interneuron gamma) mechanisms in an excitatory-inhibitory network. Theta-frequency external drive to the inhibitory population switches the network between these two rhythms. Next, we build canonical interhemispheric circuits, composed of two such excitatory-inhibitory modules, delay-coupled across hemispheres. These circuits switch between in-phase gamma and anti-phase splines within a single theta cycle, reproducing the cross-spectral statistics of experimental RSG recordings. Finally, we present analytical results for threshold-linear neural mass models, showing cross-hemispheric phase patterning is governed by the ratio of cross-hemispheric delay to local inhibitory delay; we obtain explicit ranges of this ratio for which RSG-like patterning could be expected. Our work establishes that the unique oscillatory profile of RSG can be explained parsimoniously by minimal interhemispheric circuit configurations and provides a framework for experimental interrogation of interhemispheric rhythms.

papers.title: Evolutionary tuning of complexin-synaptotagmin fusion clamp governs regulated neurotransmitter release
papers.abstract: Synaptic vesicles must be held in a fusion-ready but restrained state until calcium influx triggers release. Synaptotagmin-1 (Syt1) and Complexin (CPX) both contribute to this fusion clamp, yet removing either protein produces opposite effects in different species. Whether this reflects genuine divergence in their molecular roles, or species-specific tuning of a conserved mechanism, has remained unresolved. Here we address this by comparing mammalian and C. elegans orthologs in a reconstituted single-vesicle assay that isolates clamping from upstream docking and priming. We find that clamping in both species requires the combined action of CPX and Syt1, with neither sufficient on its own. CPX clamps only with its cognate SNARE complex, a specificity conferred entirely by its accessory helix. The Syt1 orthologs differ markedly in intrinsic clamping strength, which maps to C2B mediated higher-order oligomerization and sets the functional dependence on CPX in each system. These results support a dual-regulator model of exocytosis in which Syt1 and CPX act sequentially and cooperatively through discrete molecular states to control vesicle clamping and calcium-triggered release. This framework reconciles long-standing functional discrepancies across species and reveals how evolutionary divergence modulates conserved mechanisms governing synaptic fidelity.

papers.title: Comparative Proteomics Reveals Cell-Type-Specific Heterogeneity of Human Neural Cell-Derived Extracellular Vesicles
papers.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly explored as biomarkers and as drug delivery vehicles for the brain, yet how EV cargo differs among neural cell types at baseline remains poorly defined. This gap limits both the interpretation of disease-associated EV changes and the rational choice of EV source for therapeutic use. Here, we compared EVs from human neuronal-like SH-SY5Y cells (N-EV), astrocytes (AS-EV), and HMC3 microglia (MG-EV) side by side using tandem mass tag (TMT)-based quantitative proteomics, with all samples analyzed in a single multiplexed batch. EV identity was supported by TEM, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and canonical MISEV2023 markers. Size, zeta potential, and protein content per vesicle were comparable across EV types, whereas N-EV showed the highest particle concentration and protein yield. Enrichment analyses and consensus clustering showed cargo consistent with parental-cell functions: neuronal connectivity and structural remodeling in N-EV, extracellular support and cellular interaction in AS-EV, and immune surveillance in MG-EV. Cross-comparison also revealed patterns beyond these canonical roles, including complement-associated cargo shared by N-EV and MG-EV and a Glial-EV signature of chromatin-associated and epigenetic regulatory proteins shared by AS-EV and MG-EV. We further defined cell-type-specific signature proteins; interaction networks of the larger sets were consistent with the enrichment results. Overall, these data provide a baseline comparative reference of EV proteomes from human neural cell models for interpreting disease-associated alterations, selecting EV sources for therapeutic use, and generating hypotheses on selective cargo sorting.

papers.title: Neural mechanisms for resilient sensory computation under metabolic stress
papers.abstract: Food-restricted mice can solve visual discrimination tasks despite reduced synaptic currents and increased noise resulting from cellular changes in the primary visual cortex. Combining neural recordings and modeling, we study the population structure of the noise and show it is mainly concentrated along task-irrelevant directions in high-dimensional population activity, hence preserving coding on the low-dimensional stimulus manifold. In addition, we predict that food restriction shortens decision times, conserving energy but limiting the evidence accumulation needed for fine discrimination.

papers.title: Pregnancy History and Loss of Normal PSEN2 Function Impact Female Late-Life Cognitive Processing, Inhibitory Signaling, and Gliosis
papers.abstract: Background. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is well-documented to be more progressive in affected females. It is thus critical to define how female-specific life experiences interact with AD-related risk factors to impact disease trajectory and functional burden. For example, pregnancy exerts dramatic influences on the maternal immune system, behavior, and neuroplasticity, specifically in hippocampal and limbic structures. The long-term clinical impacts from pregnancy history (parity) on late-life AD outcomes are, however, conflicting. Thus, we investigated the late-life functional impacts of parity on rodent cognitive function, inhibitory neuron density, and glial biology with loss of normal function of the AD-related risk factor, presenilin 2 (PSEN2). Methods. Female PSEN2 knockout (KO) and wild-type (WT) mice with (multiparous) and without (nulliparous) pregnancy history were challenged at 10-15 months-old in the T-maze (TM) and Open Field Test (OFT), followed by immunofluorescence for neuronal signaling and gliosis markers. Results. Neither parity history nor PSEN2 deficiency impacted hippocampally-mediated spatial working memory of aged female mice in the TM. However, both PSEN2 KO and multiparous mice exhibited decreased OFT locomotor behavior. Multiparous mice also showed reduced OFT center zone exploration (p=0.0045) suggesting a more anxious phenotype. Parity history generally increased inhibitory marker expression in dorsal hippocampus (p=0.017), prefrontal cortex (p=0.021), and amygdala (p=0.035). Parity generally blunted oligodendrocyte marker expression in CA1 (p<0.05), while boosting astrocyte and microglia marker expression in CA3 of dorsal hippocampus. Conclusion. This work suggests that although parity history and PSEN2 deficiency exert individual differing age-related effects on cognition and neurobiology, they do not act synergistically.
